Warsh Suggests Fed Rate Hike Is Good-News Story, Touting Growth | Fed Chair Warsh sells rate hike as a reflection of a strengthening economy Why did Trump's "hand-picked" Fed chair defy him by raising interest rates? The Federal Reserve's institutional independence is facing a critical structural test following the FOMC's unanimous decision to hike benchmark interest rates by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%–4.00%. This unexpected tightening directly defies intense public pressure from President Trump, who heavily lobbied his newly appointed Fed Chair, Kevin Warsh, for deep rate cuts to "1% or less." With a sticky 3.4% inflation that was supercharged by surging global fuel prices from the US-Israel conflict with Iran, Warsh and the board chose to defend the central bank’s 2% inflation mandate over political expediency. This sudden pivot—that landed just 48 days before US midterm elections—setting up a showdown between White House fiscal goals and a restrictive central bank. Warsh framed this rate hike as a "good-news story," touting that strong economic growth prospects and a resilient labor market gave them the perfect runway to tighten safely. He unanimously chose to defend institutional credibility over short-term political cycles — Is the Fed successfully insulating macroeconomic stability from political cycles, or will tightening into a geopolitical supply-side shock inadvertently trigger stagflation? 10-year Treasury yield hits highest level since 2002 as global bond rout gathers pace Government borrowing costs rose around the world on Thursday, continuing a months-long trend as investors express concerns over a lack of political action to tackle fiscal deficits, while inflation remains sticky and interest rates rise.

Feds to buy up to $6 billion in Treasury bonds in move to ease borrowing costs U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday that the agency will buy up to $6 billion in long-term government bonds as part of an effort to curb rising yields and ease borrowing costs. The Treasury Department vowed last month to "at least" double its bond buybacks to $4 billion to prop up prices. Higher Treasury yields raise borrowing costs for consumers and businesses, and can also weigh on stock prices. Rising U.S. government debt is the main catalyst driving up bond yields, O'Rourke added. The national debt surpassed $40 trillion in August after doubling in less than a decade. "If you want to get Treasury yields under control, you would tackle that issue. Instead, we are tinkering on the periphery of the market, and that's not a real solution," said Mike O'Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading. Columbia Business School economist Brett House told CBS News the bond buyback "doesn't solve the fact that the U.S. is running a large deficit that needs to be financed." "Unless Bessent forces the Fed to print money to buy these bonds, it is still coming out of Treasury revenues, and doesn't cure the fact that this government is building up a deficit and as a result is going to have to issue more debt," he added. The 10-year Treasury rate, which typically affects mortgage rates, rose to 4.85% from 4.80% late Tuesday, hitting its highest point since October 2023.
